Our companions (the grammarians of the Basran school) call what al-Zamakhshari denied suspension, and they say that when a verb transitive to two objects takes the first as its object and is followed by an interrogative clause, or by the lam of commencement, or by a negative particle, the clause is the one suspended from the verb, and it stands in the accusative position, as if it occupied the position of the two objects, and in it is what suspends the verb from governing. (p-298) The discussion of this type of clause has already been given in al-Kahf, in His saying: ﴿That He may test them, which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

(Tibaqan) is in the accusative as an attribute of (seven). It is either a verbal noun of (taba-qa), "to match closely," from the saying "the sandal, its soles are layered one upon another," and it is described by it for the sake of emphasis; or it is a construct with an omitted noun, meaning "possessing layers"; or it is a plural of (tabaq), like (jamal) and (jimal), or a plural of (tabaqa), like (rahaba) and (rihab). The meaning is that some are above others. As for what is mentioned concerning the materials of these heavens: the first is of a wave held in check, the second of white pearl, the third of iron, the fourth of copper, the fifth of silver, the sixth of gold, and the seventh of white emerald. This requires an authentic transmission. Some who claimed piety, who was blind and could not see the place of his foot, reported that he was observing the heavens with some of the attributes we have mentioned.

(Tafawut): Ibn Abbas said: "division." al-Suddi said: "fault." 'Ata' ibn Yasar said: "lack of evenness." Tha'lab said: its root is from (fawt), which is for one thing to pass another in terms of defect. It has been said: "disturbance." It has been said: "crookedness." It has been said: "contradiction." It has been said: "disagreement." It has been said: "lack of proportion." Tafawut means exceeding the limit at which an increase or a decrease would be required. One of the men of letters said:

"Its limbs are proportioned; you see no disagreement among them, but they came in measure."

The majority recited (min tafawut) with an alif, the verbal noun of (tafawata). Abd Allah, 'Alqama, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Talha and al-A'mash read it with a doubled waw, as the verbal noun of (tafawwata). Abu Zayd ibn al-Arabi reported (tafawutan) with a damma, fatha and kasra on the waw, and the fatha and kasra are irregular. The apparent meaning is that the generality of "the creation of the Most Merciful" includes the spheres and other things, for there is no defect or rift in it; rather, everything operates in perfect precision. It has been said: what is meant by "the creation of the Most Merciful" is the heavens alone. The apparent meaning is that His saying, "you see," is a resumptive statement that there is no discrepancy in His creation, may He be exalted. Al-Zamakhshari made this clause a qualifying attribute following (tibaqan). Its original form is "you see no discrepancy in them," but in place of the pronoun he put "the creation of the Most Merciful," to magnify their creation and to draw attention to the cause of their freedom from discrepancy, namely that it is the creation of the Most Merciful, and that He, by His overwhelming power, is the One who creates such a fitting creation. End of quotation. The address in (tara) is to every addressee, or to the Messenger (ﷺ). When He informed that there is no discrepancy in His creation, He commanded the repeated looking at the fitting creation, saying: (look again). In the fa' there is a meaning of causation: the eye corresponds to what was reported.

(Futur): Mujahid said: "cracks." (Fatara) of a camel's tooth means it split the flesh and appeared. The poet said:

"He built for you a sky without pillars, and He made it level, and there is no rift in it."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "gaps." He cited the verse of Ubayd ibn Mas'ud:

"I split the heart, then I returned into it your love, so it was cracked, and the rift was closed."

al-Suddi said: "holes." Qatada said: "flaws"; from this come (tafṭir) and (infitar). Ibn Abbas said: "weakness." These explanations are close in meaning.

The clause (hal tara min futur) is in the accusative position, governed by a suspended verb deleted in the estimate: "so look, do you see...?" Or the meaning of "look" (fa-rji' al-basar) has been construed as "look with your eye, do you see...?" in which case it is suspended.

(Then look again) means repeat it. (Twice) is a dual, but it is not meant as a pair of one; rather it is meant as repetition, as if He said: one time after another, meaning many times, like His saying (labbayka), meaning many responses in succession. The dual is used to mean multiplicity, just as what is its root is used to mean multiplicity, and it is a singular joined to a singular, as in the verse:

"If a grave and a grave were counted, he would be the most honoured of them in house, and the farthest from the abode of the visitor."

He means: if many graves were counted. Ibn Atiyya and others said: (kartayn) means "twice," and it is accusative as an absolute object. It has been said: He commanded the return of sight to the sky twice; the first time he made an error, so he corrected it with the second. It has been said: the first is so that he might see its beauty and evenness, and the second so that he might see its stars in their course and their ending.

The majority read (yanqalib) in the jussive, as the answer to the imperative. al-Khwarazmi reported from al-Kisa'i that it is in the nominative, meaning "then it returns," with the fa' omitted, or as the position of a hypothetical circumstantial clause: if you return your sight and repeat the gaze, seeking a rift, a crack, or a defect, it will return to you removed from what you sought, because there is none of it in them; and it is weary from the abundance of looking. Its weariness indicates that (the two times) does not mean a pair of one, for the sight does not become weary by looking twice. (Hasir) means weary, as the poet said:

"Their hooves, though they were no help against the distance, and there remains among them a lame and worn-out one."

It is said: his camel became worn out (hasara, yahsiru, husur), meaning it grew weary and cut off, so it is (hasir) and (mahsur). The poet describing a she-camel said:

"Half of her is a gaze of the two eyes, worn out."

That is, her neck. (Hasir) in the sense of "weary, exhausted" has also been pluralized, as the poet said:

"With them are the carcasses of the exhausted, as for their bones..." the verse.

The lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya) is the one we see. Nearness is a relative matter; otherwise it is not near. (With lamps): that is, with stars shining like lamps. (Masabih) is an absolute term for lights, so it does not indicate that the heavens other than the lowest have no lamps. (And We made them missiles against the devils): that is, We made from them; for the heaven itself is not what is pelted with the projectiles. This holds if the pronoun in (wa ja'alnaha) refers to the heaven. The apparent reference is to (masabih). He attributed the pelting to them because the meteor that follows the eavesdropper is separated from their fire, while the stars remain fixed in His dominion in their state. The meteor is like a brand taken from the fire, and the fire remains and does not diminish. The apparent meaning is that the devils are the eavesdroppers on the hearing, and that the pelting is a real event in which they are struck with meteors, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Hijr and Surat al-Saffat. It has also been said: the meaning of (rujum) is "conjectures" directed at the human devils, who are the astrologers. They attribute to the stars things by way of conjecture from their ignorant ones, and by fabrication and invention from their cunning ones. They have in this matter compositions containing superstitions with which they deceive kings and weak minds, and they draw up horoscopes in which they pronounce judgments on matters, none of which turns out correct. We have come upon some of their lies in those horoscopes, and what they relate from Abu Ma'shar and others of the wicked shaykhs is falsehood by which they mislead ignorant people. Qatada said: God, may He be exalted, created the stars as an adornment for the heaven, as pelting for the devils, and as guidance by which people find their way on land and sea. Whoever claims anything other than these three qualities has overstepped and forfeited his share of the Hereafter. The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the devils.

The Qur'an reader (qāri') Ḥamzah... no, the majority of reciters (al-Jumhūr) read ʿadhābu Jahannama with a raised bāʾ (ʿadhābu, nominative). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Aʿraj, Usayd ibn Usayd al-Muzanī, and al-Ḥasan, in the transmission of Hārūn from him, read it in the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction with ʿadhāba al-saʿīr (the blazing punishment), meaning: "And We have prepared for those who disbelieve the punishment of Jahannam (Hell)." ﴿When they are cast into it﴾, i.e., thrown in, just as firewood is thrown into a great fire and hurled into it, and a similar usage is ﴿the fuel of Jahannam﴾. ﴿They will hear from it﴾, i.e., from Jahannam, ﴿a roaring (shahīq)﴾, meaning a hideous sound like the braying of a donkey, because of its intense blazing and seething. It is possible that this is an elision of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning: they will hear the roaring of its inhabitants, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and roaring﴾ [Hud: 106]. ﴿And it boils up, seething with them like a cauldron.﴾ ﴿It nearly bursts with rage (tamayyaz)﴾, i.e., parts of it separate from one another because of its violent agitation. It is said: "So-and-so bursts (yatamayyaz) with rage," when people describe someone as extremely angry.

The majority read tamayyaz with a single light tāʾ. Al-Bazzī read it with a shadda (doubled letter). Ṭalḥah read it with two tāʾs. Abū ʿAmr read it with assimilation of the dāl into the tāʾ. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read tamāyaz on the pattern tafāʿala, whose underlying form is tatamāyaz with two tāʾs. Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read tamīz, from māza min al-ghayẓ (he was enraged) at the disbelievers. It is figuratively treated as if it were enraged at them because of its intense seething against them. A similar figurative usage appears in the verse of the poet about the dog (Kalb):

*It runs with such vigor that it nearly leaps out of its skin.*

And the saying of people: "So-and-so became angry, and a part of him flew off to the earth and a part to the sky," when he is extremely enraged. It is also possible that the meaning is the rage of the guardians of Hell (al-zabāniyah). ﴿Every time a group (fawj) is cast into it﴾, i.e., a company of disbelievers, its keepers (khazanah) ask them a question of rebuke and reproach, and this itself increases their punishment over their punishment. Its keepers are Mālik and his assistants: ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ who would warn you of this Day? ﴿They say: "Yes"﴾, an acknowledgment of the arrival of the warners to them.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is their acknowledgment of the justice of God, and their confession that He, Mighty and Exalted, removed their excuses by sending the Messengers and warning them about what they fell into, and that they were not afflicted by any lack of ability, as the al-Mujbirah (determinists, Jabriyyah) claim, but came about only from themselves and their own choice, contrary to what God chose and commanded and threatened for its opposite. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Muʿtazilah (the rationalist school). The apparent meaning is that the words ﴿You are only in great error﴾ are the words of the disbelievers to the Messengers who came to them as warners. They first denied that God had sent down anything, then they mocked the one who reported that God, may He be exalted, had sent Messengers to them, and that the one who says this is in a great bewilderment. It is also possible that these are the words of the guardians to the disbelievers, informing and rebuking them about what they used to be in the world. They meant by "error" the destruction they were in, or they called the punishment of error "error" because it arose from error. Al-Zamakhsharī also said: Or they are the words of the Messengers to them, relayed to the guardians, meaning: they said to us this, and we did not accept it. End of quotation. If the address in ﴿You are only in error﴾ is to the Messengers, it may be intended generically, and that is why the address is in the plural.

﴿And they say﴾, i.e., to the guardians when they debated with them: ﴿If only we had listened (lau kunnā nasmaʿu) like one seeking the truth, or reasoned (naʿqilu) like one who reflects upon it, we would not have deserved to be in the Fire forever.﴾ So they acknowledged their sin, i.e., their denial of the Messengers. ﴿So away (fa-suḥqan)!﴾ i.e., far away with them. This is a supplication against them. Suḥq means distance. Its position is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: God distanced them, a distancing. The poet said:

*He roams the far corners of the lands, a wanderer,*
*and the east wind scatters him in every direction.*

Its verb is triliteral (thulāthī). Al-Zajjāj said: meaning, God distanced them, i.e., He placed them far away. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the analogical form would be isḥāq, but the verbal noun came with elision, as is said in the verse:

*And if I perish, that was my decree,*

meaning, my decree. End of quotation. But there is no need to claim elision in the verbal noun, since its verb has come in triliteral form, as the poet recited: *and the east wind scatters him in every direction.*

The majority read the ḥāʾ with a sukūn (suḥqan). ʿAlī, Abū Jaʿfar, and al-Kisāʾī, with a variant from Abū al-Ḥārith on his authority, read it with a ḍamma (suḥuqan). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "fa-suḥqan" is in the accusative as a supplication against them, and this is permissible here, because on God's part, this statement about them is established at first, and its actual occurrence will not happen except in the Hereafter, so it is, for that reason, in the category of what is anticipated and prayed for, just as you say: "Far away with Zayd, and distant." The accusative in all of this is by an implied verb. If it occurs and is established, the proper form is the nominative, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 1], and ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, and other examples. End of quotation.

﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen﴾, i.e., the matter of the Return and its conditions which they were informed of, or unseen from people's eyes, i.e., in their solitude, as in His saying (ﷺ): "And a man who remembered God in seclusion, and his eyes overflowed." ﴿And keep your speech secret or divulge it﴾, addressed to all creation. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The occasion of its revelation was that some polytheists said to others: "Keep your speech secret, lest the God of Muḥammad hear you." ﴿Does He not know, He who created?﴾ The hamza is an interrogative particle, and "lā" is a negation. The apparent reading is that "man" (whoever) is the object (maf'ūl), and the meaning is: Would His knowledge of whom He created be negated? He is the One whose knowledge is subtle and profound, who encompasses hidden and evident matters. Some grammarians permitted that "man" be the subject (fāʿil), with the object omitted, as if he said: "Does not the Creator know your secret and your open speech?" It is an interrogative with the meaning of denial, i.e., how could He not know what you speak, He who created things and brought them into existence from pure nonexistence, while He is the Subtle, the All-Aware, whose knowledge reaches what appears of His creation and what is hidden?

﴿It is He who made the earth subservient (dhalūlan) for you﴾. This is a favor from Him, exalted, by that. Dhalūl is an intensive form (fa'ūl) from that root: you say "a tame (dhalūl) mount," meaning clearly subdued, and "a humble (dhalīl) man," meaning clearly humbled. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Dhalūl is fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl, i.e., "made tame" (madhlūlah), so it is like rakūb (ridden) and ḥalūb (milked). End of quotation. But it does not mean maf'ūl, because its verb is intransitive, and it is transitive only with the hamza, as in His saying: "and You humble whom You will," or with the doubling (taḍʿīf), as in His saying: "and We made them subservient to them." His saying, meaning "made tame," appears to be an error.

﴿So walk in its corners﴾: a command to make use of it and to earn from it. As for its corners (manākibihā), Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Bishr ibn Kaʿb said: its edges, and these are the mountains. Al-Farrāʾ, al-Kalbī, and Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: its sides. The "manakib" of a man are his two sides. Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: its extremities and its paths. Al-Zamakhsharī said: Walking in its corners is a metaphor for extreme subjugation and going beyond the limit, because the two shoulders of a camel and the point where they meet from the withers are the most delicate part of a camel, and the least suited to being stepped upon by a rider and leaned upon. So when He makes it so subdued that one walks in its corners, it does not ascend. End of quotation. Al-Zajjāj said: He made the traveling through its mountains easy for you, and this is the most eloquent form of subjugation.

﴿And to Him is the resurrection (nushūr)﴾, i.e., the raising from the dead, so He will ask you about thanking Him for this blessing.

(Surah al-Mulk is Meccan, and it has thirty verses.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿He who created death and life that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed; and He is the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers. You see no discord in the creation of the Most Merciful. Look again: do you see any rift?﴾ ﴿Then look again, twice; your sight will return to you humbled and weary.﴾ ﴿We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils, and for them We have prepared the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿For those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿When they are thrown into it, they hear its roaring as it boils up,﴾ ﴿almost bursting with rage. Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them: "Did no warner come to you?"﴾ ﴿They say: "Yes, a warner came to us, but we denied him and said: God has revealed nothing. You are only in great error."﴾ ﴿And they say: "Had we listened or understood, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze."﴾ ﴿So they confess their sin. Away with the companions of the Blaze!﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen, for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ ﴿Keep your speech secret or make it public; indeed He knows what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.﴾ ﴿He it is who made the earth subservient to you, so walk in its tracts and eat of His provision; and to Him is the resurrection.﴾

(p-297) This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is this: when the two women who were destined for wretchedness were set forth as an example for the disbelievers, though they were under two prophets, and when Asiya and Maryam were set forth as an example for the believers, though both were destined for Paradise, even though their peoples were disbelievers, this was a disposal of His dominion according to what had already been decreed. So He said: (Blessed) meaning exalted and magnified is He in whose hand is the dominion. This is a metaphor for comprehensive power and irresistible authority. The attribution of a hand to Him, may He be exalted, occurs frequently, as in His saying: ﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the sovereignty of all things﴾ [Ya-Sin: 83], and ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾. With respect to Him, the hand is a metaphor (isti'ara) for establishing sovereignty, since among people it is an instrument of possession. Here the dominion is absolute; it does not perish or fail. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that it means the King of kings, based on His saying: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of Sovereignty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Mention of the attribute of power and of life is appropriate to the dominion, since perception is valid only through their existence. The meaning of His creating death is bringing into existence that which makes death possible and bringing about its occurrence. The meaning is: He created your death and your life, O you who are accountable. He called the knowledge of what actually occurs from them by their own choice a trial (bala), which is bewilderment, using a metaphor from the act of one who tests. In a hadith, it is explained that (which of you is best in deed) means who has the best intellect, the greatest fear (of God), and the best judgment regarding His commands and prohibitions, even if he is least in voluntary acts of worship. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Thawri that it means the one most ascetic in this world. It has also been said: death is used as a metaphor for this world, since death occurs within it, and life for the Hereafter, since there is no death in it. So it is as if He said: He it is who created this world and the Hereafter. He described them by two verbal nouns, and He placed death first because it is more awe-inspiring to souls.

(liyabluwakum) is connected to (created). (Which of you is best in deed) is a subject and predicate. Al-Hawfi estimated a verb before it, so that the clause would occupy the position of its object, and it is suspended (mu'allaq) from it. Its estimate is: "so He looks." Ibn Atiyya estimated: "so He looks" or "so He knows."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, how does the phrase (which of you is best in deed) relate to the verb of trial?" I answer: because it contains the meaning of knowledge; it is as if it were said: "that He may know which of you is best in deed." When you say, "I know whether Zayd is best in deed or he is," this clause occupies the position of the second of its two objects, just as you say, "I know him to be best in deed." If you ask, "Is this called suspension (ta'liq)?" I answer: No. Suspension is when you place after it something that fills the position of both objects together, as in your saying, "I know which of them is 'Amr," and "I know whether Zayd is departing." Do you not see that after one of the two objects has been stated, there is no difference between what follows being introduced by an interrogative particle and not being introduced by it? If it were suspension, the two situations would differ, just as they differ in your saying, "I know whether Zayd is departing," and "I know Zayd to be departing." End of quotation. Our companions (the grammarians of the Basran school) call what al-Zamakhshari denied suspension, and they say that when a verb transitive to two objects takes the first as its object and is followed by an interrogative clause, or by the lam of commencement, or by a negative particle, the clause is the one suspended from the verb, and it stands in the accusative position, as if it occupied the position of the two objects, and in it is what suspends the verb from governing. (p-298) The discussion of this type of clause has already been given in al-Kahf, in His saying: ﴿That He may test them, which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

It has been said: He commanded the return of sight to the sky twice; the first time he made an error, so he corrected it with the second. It has been said: the first is so that he might see its beauty and evenness, and the second so that he might see its stars in their course and their ending.

The majority read (yanqalib) in the jussive, as the answer to the imperative. al-Khwarazmi reported from al-Kisa'i that it is in the nominative, meaning "then it returns," with the fa' omitted, or as the position of a hypothetical circumstantial clause: if you return your sight and repeat the gaze, seeking a rift, a crack, or a defect, it will return to you removed from what you sought, because there is none of it in them; and it is weary from the abundance of looking. Its weariness indicates that (the two times) does not mean a pair of one, for the sight does not become weary by looking twice. (Hasir) means weary, as the poet said:

"Their hooves, though they were no help against the distance, and there remains among them a lame and worn-out one."

It is said: his camel became worn out (hasara, yahsiru, husur), meaning it grew weary and cut off, so it is (hasir) and (mahsur). The poet describing a she-camel said:

"Half of her is a gaze of the two eyes, worn out."

That is, her neck. (Hasir) in the sense of "weary, exhausted" has also been pluralized, as the poet said:

"With them are the carcasses of the exhausted, as for their bones..." the verse.

The lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya) is the one we see. Nearness is a relative matter; otherwise it is not near. (With lamps): that is, with stars shining like lamps. (Masabih) is an absolute term for lights, so it does not indicate that the heavens other than the lowest have no lamps. (And We made them missiles against the devils): that is, We made from them; for the heaven itself is not what is pelted with the projectiles. This holds if the pronoun in (wa ja'alnaha) refers to the heaven. The apparent reference is to (masabih). He attributed the pelting to them because the meteor that follows the eavesdropper is separated from their fire, while the stars remain fixed in His dominion in their state. The meteor is like a brand taken from the fire, and the fire remains and does not diminish. The apparent meaning is that the devils are the eavesdroppers on the hearing, and that the pelting is a real event in which they are struck with meteors, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Hijr and Surat al-Saffat. It has also been said: the meaning of (rujum) is "conjectures" directed at the human devils, who are the astrologers. They attribute to the stars things by way of conjecture from their ignorant ones, and by fabrication and invention from their cunning ones. They have in this matter compositions containing superstitions with which they deceive kings and weak minds, and they draw up horoscopes in which they pronounce judgments on matters, none of which turns out correct. We have come upon some of their lies in those horoscopes, and what they relate from Abu Ma'shar and others of the wicked shaykhs is falsehood by which they mislead ignorant people. Qatada said: God, may He be exalted, created the stars as an adornment for the heaven, as pelting for the devils, and as guidance by which people find their way on land and sea. Whoever claims anything other than these three qualities has overstepped and forfeited his share of the Hereafter. The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the devils.

The Qur'an reader (qāri') Ḥamzah... no, the majority of reciters (al-Jumhūr) read ʿadhābu Jahannama with a raised bāʾ (ʿadhābu, nominative). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Aʿraj, Usayd ibn Usayd al-Muzanī, and al-Ḥasan, in the transmission of Hārūn from him, read it in the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction with ʿadhāba al-saʿīr (the blazing punishment), meaning: "And We have prepared for those who disbelieve the punishment of Jahannam (Hell)." ﴿When they are cast into it﴾, i.e., thrown in, just as firewood is thrown into a great fire and hurled into it, and a similar usage is ﴿the fuel of Jahannam﴾. ﴿They will hear from it﴾, i.e., from Jahannam, ﴿a roaring (shahīq)﴾, meaning a hideous sound like the braying of a donkey, because of its intense blazing and seething. It is possible that this is an elision of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), meaning: they will hear the roaring of its inhabitants, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿For them therein is groaning and roaring﴾ [Hud: 106]. ﴿And it boils up, seething with them like a cauldron.﴾ ﴿It nearly bursts with rage (tamayyaz)﴾, i.e., parts of it separate from one another because of its violent agitation. It is said: "So-and-so bursts (yatamayyaz) with rage," when people describe someone as extremely angry.

The majority read tamayyaz with a single light tāʾ. Al-Bazzī read it with a shadda (doubled letter). Ṭalḥah read it with two tāʾs. Abū ʿAmr read it with assimilation of the dāl into the tāʾ. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read tamāyaz on the pattern tafāʿala, whose underlying form is tatamāyaz with two tāʾs. Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read tamīz, from māza min al-ghayẓ (he was enraged) at the disbelievers. It is figuratively treated as if it were enraged at them because of its intense seething against them. A similar figurative usage appears in the verse of the poet about the dog (Kalb):

*It runs with such vigor that it nearly leaps out of its skin.*

And the saying of people: "So-and-so became angry, and a part of him flew off to the earth and a part to the sky," when he is extremely enraged. It is also possible that the meaning is the rage of the guardians of Hell (al-zabāniyah). ﴿Every time a group (fawj) is cast into it﴾, i.e., a company of disbelievers, its keepers (khazanah) ask them a question of rebuke and reproach, and this itself increases their punishment over their punishment. Its keepers are Mālik and his assistants: ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ who would warn you of this Day? ﴿They say: "Yes"﴾, an acknowledgment of the arrival of the warners to them.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is their acknowledgment of the justice of God, and their confession that He, Mighty and Exalted, removed their excuses by sending the Messengers and warning them about what they fell into, and that they were not afflicted by any lack of ability, as the al-Mujbirah (determinists, Jabriyyah) claim, but came about only from themselves and their own choice, contrary to what God chose and commanded and threatened for its opposite. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Muʿtazilah (the rationalist school). The apparent meaning is that the words ﴿You are only in great error﴾ are the words of the disbelievers to the Messengers who came to them as warners. They first denied that God had sent down anything, then they mocked the one who reported that God, may He be exalted, had sent Messengers to them, and that the one who says this is in a great bewilderment. It is also possible that these are the words of the guardians to the disbelievers, informing and rebuking them about what they used to be in the world. They meant by "error" the destruction they were in, or they called the punishment of error "error" because it arose from error. Al-Zamakhsharī also said: Or they are the words of the Messengers to them, relayed to the guardians, meaning: they said to us this, and we did not accept it. End of quotation. If the address in ﴿You are only in error﴾ is to the Messengers, it may be intended generically, and that is why the address is in the plural.

﴿And they say﴾, i.e., to the guardians when they debated with them: ﴿If only we had listened (lau kunnā nasmaʿu) like one seeking the truth, or reasoned (naʿqilu) like one who reflects upon it, we would not have deserved to be in the Fire forever.﴾ So they acknowledged their sin, i.e., their denial of the Messengers. ﴿So away (fa-suḥqan)!﴾ i.e., far away with them. This is a supplication against them. Suḥq means distance. Its position is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: God distanced them, a distancing. The poet said:

*He roams the far corners of the lands, a wanderer,*
*and the east wind scatters him in every direction.*

Its verb is triliteral (thulāthī). Al-Zajjāj said: meaning, God distanced them, i.e., He placed them far away. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the analogical form would be isḥāq, but the verbal noun came with elision, as is said in the verse:

*And if I perish, that was my decree,*

meaning, my decree. End of quotation. But there is no need to claim elision in the verbal noun, since its verb has come in triliteral form, as the poet recited: *and the east wind scatters him in every direction.*

The majority read the ḥāʾ with a sukūn (suḥqan). ʿAlī, Abū Jaʿfar, and al-Kisāʾī, with a variant from Abū al-Ḥārith on his authority, read it with a ḍamma (suḥuqan). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "fa-suḥqan" is in the accusative as a supplication against them, and this is permissible here, because on God's part, this statement about them is established at first, and its actual occurrence will not happen except in the Hereafter, so it is, for that reason, in the category of what is anticipated and prayed for, just as you say: "Far away with Zayd, and distant." The accusative in all of this is by an implied verb. If it occurs and is established, the proper form is the nominative, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 1], and ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, and other examples. End of quotation.

﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen﴾, i.e., the matter of the Return and its conditions which they were informed of, or unseen from people's eyes, i.e., in their solitude, as in His saying (ﷺ): "And a man who remembered God in seclusion, and his eyes overflowed." ﴿And keep your speech secret or divulge it﴾, addressed to all creation. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The occasion of its revelation was that some polytheists said to others: "Keep your speech secret, lest the God of Muḥammad hear you." ﴿Does He not know, He who created?﴾ The hamza is an interrogative particle, and "lā" is a negation. The apparent reading is that "man" (whoever) is the object (maf'ūl), and the meaning is: Would His knowledge of whom He created be negated? He is the One whose knowledge is subtle and profound, who encompasses hidden and evident matters. Some grammarians permitted that "man" be the subject (fāʿil), with the object omitted, as if he said: "Does not the Creator know your secret and your open speech?" It is an interrogative with the meaning of denial, i.e., how could He not know what you speak, He who created things and brought them into existence from pure nonexistence, while He is the Subtle, the All-Aware, whose knowledge reaches what appears of His creation and what is hidden?

﴿It is He who made the earth subservient (dhalūlan) for you﴾. This is a favor from Him, exalted, by that. Dhalūl is an intensive form (fa'ūl) from that root: you say "a tame (dhalūl) mount," meaning clearly subdued, and "a humble (dhalīl) man," meaning clearly humbled. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Dhalūl is fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl, i.e., "made tame" (madhlūlah), so it is like rakūb (ridden) and ḥalūb (milked). End of quotation. But it does not mean maf'ūl, because its verb is intransitive, and it is transitive only with the hamza, as in His saying: "and You humble whom You will," or with the doubling (taḍʿīf), as in His saying: "and We made them subservient to them." His saying, meaning "made tame," appears to be an error.

﴿So walk in its corners﴾: a command to make use of it and to earn from it. As for its corners (manākibihā), Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Bishr ibn Kaʿb said: its edges, and these are the mountains. Al-Farrāʾ, al-Kalbī, and Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: its sides. The "manakib" of a man are his two sides. Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: its extremities and its paths. Al-Zamakhsharī said: Walking in its corners is a metaphor for extreme subjugation and going beyond the limit, because the two shoulders of a camel and the point where they meet from the withers are the most delicate part of a camel, and the least suited to being stepped upon by a rider and leaned upon. So when He makes it so subdued that one walks in its corners, it does not ascend. End of quotation. Al-Zajjāj said: He made the traveling through its mountains easy for you, and this is the most eloquent form of subjugation.

﴿And to Him is the resurrection (nushūr)﴾, i.e., the raising from the dead, so He will ask you about thanking Him for this blessing.

(Surah al-Mulk is Meccan, and it has thirty verses.)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿He who created death and life that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed; and He is the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers. You see no discord in the creation of the Most Merciful. Look again: do you see any rift?﴾ ﴿Then look again, twice; your sight will return to you humbled and weary.﴾ ﴿We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils, and for them We have prepared the punishment of the Blaze.﴾ ﴿For those who disbelieve in their Lord is the punishment of Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ ﴿When they are thrown into it, they hear its roaring as it boils up,﴾ ﴿almost bursting with rage. Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them: "Did no warner come to you?"﴾ ﴿They say: "Yes, a warner came to us, but we denied him and said: God has revealed nothing. You are only in great error."﴾ ﴿And they say: "Had we listened or understood, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze."﴾ ﴿So they confess their sin. Away with the companions of the Blaze!﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen, for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ ﴿Keep your speech secret or make it public; indeed He knows what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware.﴾ ﴿He it is who made the earth subservient to you, so walk in its tracts and eat of His provision; and to Him is the resurrection.﴾

(p-297) This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it is this: when the two women who were destined for wretchedness were set forth as an example for the disbelievers, though they were under two prophets, and when Asiya and Maryam were set forth as an example for the believers, though both were destined for Paradise, even though their peoples were disbelievers, this was a disposal of His dominion according to what had already been decreed. So He said: (Blessed) meaning exalted and magnified is He in whose hand is the dominion. This is a metaphor for comprehensive power and irresistible authority. The attribution of a hand to Him, may He be exalted, occurs frequently, as in His saying: ﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the sovereignty of all things﴾ [Ya-Sin: 83], and ﴿In Your hand is all good﴾. With respect to Him, the hand is a metaphor (isti'ara) for establishing sovereignty, since among people it is an instrument of possession. Here the dominion is absolute; it does not perish or fail. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that it means the King of kings, based on His saying: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of Sovereignty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Mention of the attribute of power and of life is appropriate to the dominion, since perception is valid only through their existence. The meaning of His creating death is bringing into existence that which makes death possible and bringing about its occurrence. The meaning is: He created your death and your life, O you who are accountable. He called the knowledge of what actually occurs from them by their own choice a trial (bala), which is bewilderment, using a metaphor from the act of one who tests. In a hadith, it is explained that (which of you is best in deed) means who has the best intellect, the greatest fear (of God), and the best judgment regarding His commands and prohibitions, even if he is least in voluntary acts of worship. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Thawri that it means the one most ascetic in this world. It has also been said: death is used as a metaphor for this world, since death occurs within it, and life for the Hereafter, since there is no death in it. So it is as if He said: He it is who created this world and the Hereafter. He described them by two verbal nouns, and He placed death first because it is more awe-inspiring to souls.

(liyabluwakum) is connected to (created). (Which of you is best in deed) is a subject and predicate. Al-Hawfi estimated a verb before it, so that the clause would occupy the position of its object, and it is suspended (mu'allaq) from it. Its estimate is: "so He looks." Ibn Atiyya estimated: "so He looks" or "so He knows."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, how does the phrase (which of you is best in deed) relate to the verb of trial?" I answer: because it contains the meaning of knowledge; it is as if it were said: "that He may know which of you is best in deed." When you say, "I know whether Zayd is best in deed or he is," this clause occupies the position of the second of its two objects, just as you say, "I know him to be best in deed." If you ask, "Is this called suspension (ta'liq)?" I answer: No. Suspension is when you place after it something that fills the position of both objects together, as in your saying, "I know which of them is 'Amr," and "I know whether Zayd is departing." Do you not see that after one of the two objects has been stated, there is no difference between what follows being introduced by an interrogative particle and not being introduced by it? If it were suspension, the two situations would differ, just as they differ in your saying, "I know whether Zayd is departing," and "I know Zayd to be departing." End of quotation. Our companions (the grammarians of the Basran school) call what al-Zamakhshari denied suspension, and they say that when a verb transitive to two objects takes the first as its object and is followed by an interrogative clause, or by the lam of commencement, or by a negative particle, the clause is the one suspended from the verb, and it stands in the accusative position, as if it occupied the position of the two objects, and in it is what suspends the verb from governing. (p-298) The discussion of this type of clause has already been given in al-Kahf, in His saying: ﴿That He may test them, which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

(Tibaqan) is in the accusative as an attribute of (seven). It is either a verbal noun of (taba-qa), "to match closely," from the saying "the sandal, its soles are layered one upon another," and it is described by it for the sake of emphasis; or it is a construct with an omitted noun, meaning "possessing layers"; or it is a plural of (tabaq), like (jamal) and (jimal), or a plural of (tabaqa), like (rahaba) and (rihab). The meaning is that some are above others. As for what is mentioned concerning the materials of these heavens: the first is of a wave held in check, the second of white pearl, the third of iron, the fourth of copper, the fifth of silver, the sixth of gold, and the seventh of white emerald. This requires an authentic transmission. Some who claimed piety, who was blind and could not see the place of his foot, reported that he was observing the heavens with some of the attributes we have mentioned.

(Tafawut): Ibn Abbas said: "division." al-Suddi said: "fault." 'Ata' ibn Yasar said: "lack of evenness." Tha'lab said: its root is from (fawt), which is for one thing to pass another in terms of defect. It has been said: "disturbance." It has been said: "crookedness." It has been said: "contradiction." It has been said: "disagreement." It has been said: "lack of proportion." Tafawut means exceeding the limit at which an increase or a decrease would be required. One of the men of letters said:

"Its limbs are proportioned; you see no disagreement among them, but they came in measure."

The majority recited (min tafawut) with an alif, the verbal noun of (tafawata). Abd Allah, 'Alqama, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Talha and al-A'mash read it with a doubled waw, as the verbal noun of (tafawwata). Abu Zayd ibn al-Arabi reported (tafawutan) with a damma, fatha and kasra on the waw, and the fatha and kasra are irregular. The apparent meaning is that the generality of "the creation of the Most Merciful" includes the spheres and other things, for there is no defect or rift in it; rather, everything operates in perfect precision. It has been said: what is meant by "the creation of the Most Merciful" is the heavens alone. The apparent meaning is that His saying, "you see," is a resumptive statement that there is no discrepancy in His creation, may He be exalted. Al-Zamakhshari made this clause a qualifying attribute following (tibaqan). Its original form is "you see no discrepancy in them," but in place of the pronoun he put "the creation of the Most Merciful," to magnify their creation and to draw attention to the cause of their freedom from discrepancy, namely that it is the creation of the Most Merciful, and that He, by His overwhelming power, is the One who creates such a fitting creation. End of quotation. The address in (tara) is to every addressee, or to the Messenger (ﷺ). When He informed that there is no discrepancy in His creation, He commanded the repeated looking at the fitting creation, saying: (look again). In the fa' there is a meaning of causation: the eye corresponds to what was reported.

(Futur): Mujahid said: "cracks." (Fatara) of a camel's tooth means it split the flesh and appeared. The poet said:

"He built for you a sky without pillars, and He made it level, and there is no rift in it."

Abu 'Ubayda said: "gaps." He cited the verse of Ubayd ibn Mas'ud:

"I split the heart, then I returned into it your love, so it was cracked, and the rift was closed."

al-Suddi said: "holes." Qatada said: "flaws"; from this come (tafṭir) and (infitar). Ibn Abbas said: "weakness." These explanations are close in meaning.

The clause (hal tara min futur) is in the accusative position, governed by a suspended verb deleted in the estimate: "so look, do you see...?" Or the meaning of "look" (fa-rji' al-basar) has been construed as "look with your eye, do you see...?" in which case it is suspended.

(Then look again) means repeat it. (Twice) is a dual, but it is not meant as a pair of one; rather it is meant as repetition, as if He said: one time after another, meaning many times, like His saying (labbayka), meaning many responses in succession. The dual is used to mean multiplicity, just as what is its root is used to mean multiplicity, and it is a singular joined to a singular, as in the verse:

"If a grave and a grave were counted, he would be the most honoured of them in house, and the farthest from the abode of the visitor."

He means: if many graves were counted. Ibn Atiyya and others said: (kartayn) means "twice," and it is accusative as an absolute object. It has been said: He commanded the return of sight to the sky twice; the first time he made an error, so he corrected it with the second. It has been said: the first is so that he might see its beauty and evenness, and the second so that he might see its stars in their course and their ending.

"With them are the carcasses of the exhausted, as for their bones..." the verse.

It is figuratively treated as if it were enraged at them because of its intense seething against them. A similar figurative usage appears in the verse of the poet about the dog (Kalb):

*It runs with such vigor that it nearly leaps out of its skin.*

And the saying of people: "So-and-so became angry, and a part of him flew off to the earth and a part to the sky," when he is extremely enraged. It is also possible that the meaning is the rage of the guardians of Hell (al-zabāniyah). ﴿Every time a group (fawj) is cast into it﴾, i.e., a company of disbelievers, its keepers (khazanah) ask them a question of rebuke and reproach, and this itself increases their punishment over their punishment. Its keepers are Mālik and his assistants: ﴿Did no warner come to you?﴾ who would warn you of this Day? ﴿They say: "Yes"﴾, an acknowledgment of the arrival of the warners to them.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is their acknowledgment of the justice of God, and their confession that He, Mighty and Exalted, removed their excuses by sending the Messengers and warning them about what they fell into, and that they were not afflicted by any lack of ability, as the al-Mujbirah (determinists, Jabriyyah) claim, but came about only from themselves and their own choice, contrary to what God chose and commanded and threatened for its opposite. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Muʿtazilah (the rationalist school). The apparent meaning is that the words ﴿You are only in great error﴾ are the words of the disbelievers to the Messengers who came to them as warners. They first denied that God had sent down anything, then they mocked the one who reported that God, may He be exalted, had sent Messengers to them, and that the one who says this is in a great bewilderment. It is also possible that these are the words of the guardians to the disbelievers, informing and rebuking them about what they used to be in the world. They meant by "error" the destruction they were in, or they called the punishment of error "error" because it arose from error. Al-Zamakhsharī also said: Or they are the words of the Messengers to them, relayed to the guardians, meaning: they said to us this, and we did not accept it. End of quotation. If the address in ﴿You are only in error﴾ is to the Messengers, it may be intended generically, and that is why the address is in the plural.

﴿And they say﴾, i.e., to the guardians when they debated with them: ﴿If only we had listened (lau kunnā nasmaʿu) like one seeking the truth, or reasoned (naʿqilu) like one who reflects upon it, we would not have deserved to be in the Fire forever.﴾ So they acknowledged their sin, i.e., their denial of the Messengers. ﴿So away (fa-suḥqan)!﴾ i.e., far away with them. This is a supplication against them. Suḥq means distance. Its position is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: God distanced them, a distancing. The poet said:

*He roams the far corners of the lands, a wanderer,*
*and the east wind scatters him in every direction.*

Its verb is triliteral (thulāthī). Al-Zajjāj said: meaning, God distanced them, i.e., He placed them far away. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the analogical form would be isḥāq, but the verbal noun came with elision, as is said in the verse:

*And if I perish, that was my decree,*

meaning, my decree. End of quotation. But there is no need to claim elision in the verbal noun, since its verb has come in triliteral form, as the poet recited: *and the east wind scatters him in every direction.*

The majority read the ḥāʾ with a sukūn (suḥqan). ʿAlī, Abū Jaʿfar, and al-Kisāʾī, with a variant from Abū al-Ḥārith on his authority, read it with a ḍamma (suḥuqan). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "fa-suḥqan" is in the accusative as a supplication against them, and this is permissible here, because on God's part, this statement about them is established at first, and its actual occurrence will not happen except in the Hereafter, so it is, for that reason, in the category of what is anticipated and prayed for, just as you say: "Far away with Zayd, and distant." The accusative in all of this is by an implied verb. If it occurs and is established, the proper form is the nominative, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 1], and ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, and other examples. End of quotation.

﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen﴾, i.e., the matter of the Return and its conditions which they were informed of, or unseen from people's eyes, i.e., in their solitude, as in His saying (ﷺ): "And a man who remembered God in seclusion, and his eyes overflowed." ﴿And keep your speech secret or divulge it﴾, addressed to all creation. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The occasion of its revelation was that some polytheists said to others: "Keep your speech secret, lest the God of Muḥammad hear you." ﴿Does He not know, He who created?﴾ The hamza is an interrogative particle, and "lā" is a negation. The apparent reading is that "man" (whoever) is the object (maf'ūl), and the meaning is: Would His knowledge of whom He created be negated? He is the One whose knowledge is subtle and profound, who encompasses hidden and evident matters. Some grammarians permitted that "man" be the subject (fāʿil), with the object omitted, as if he said: "Does not the Creator know your secret and your open speech?" It is an interrogative with the meaning of denial, i.e., how could He not know what you speak, He who created things and brought them into existence from pure nonexistence, while He is the Subtle, the All-Aware, whose knowledge reaches what appears of His creation and what is hidden?

﴿It is He who made the earth subservient (dhalūlan) for you﴾. This is a favor from Him, exalted, by that. Dhalūl is an intensive form (fa'ūl) from that root: you say "a tame (dhalūl) mount," meaning clearly subdued, and "a humble (dhalīl) man," meaning clearly humbled. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Dhalūl is fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl, i.e., "made tame" (madhlūlah), so it is like rakūb (ridden) and ḥalūb (milked). End of quotation. But it does not mean maf'ūl, because its verb is intransitive, and it is transitive only with the hamza, as in His saying: "and You humble whom You will," or with the doubling (taḍʿīf), as in His saying: "and We made them subservient to them." His saying, meaning "made tame," appears to be an error.

﴿So walk in its corners﴾: a command to make use of it and to earn from it. As for its corners (manākibihā), Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and Bishr ibn Kaʿb said: its edges, and these are the mountains. Al-Farrāʾ, al-Kalbī, and Mundhir ibn Saʿīd said: its sides. The "manakib" of a man are his two sides. Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: its extremities and its paths. Al-Zamakhsharī said: Walking in its corners is a metaphor for extreme subjugation and going beyond the limit, because the two shoulders of a camel and the point where they meet from the withers are the most delicate part of a camel, and the least suited to being stepped upon by a rider and leaned upon. So when He makes it so subdued that one walks in its corners, it does not ascend. End of quotation. Al-Zajjāj said: He made the traveling through its mountains easy for you, and this is the most eloquent form of subjugation.

﴿And to Him is the resurrection (nushūr)﴾, i.e., the raising from the dead, so He will ask you about thanking Him for this blessing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 67, verses 16–30:

The Exalted and Majestic One said: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you, and behold, it shakes?﴾ ﴿Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send against you a violent wind (hasib), and you will know how My warning was?﴾ ﴿And those before them had denied, so how was My rejection?﴾ ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seeing of all things.﴾ ﴿Who is this that is an army for you to help you, other than the Most Merciful? The disbelievers are not but in delusion.﴾ ﴿Or who is this that provides for you if He withholds His provision? Rather, they persist in arrogance and aversion.﴾ ﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ ﴿Say: "It is He who produced you and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is He who multiplied you on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Knowledge is only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ ﴿But when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed, and it will be said, "This is what you used to call for."﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy upon us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿Say: "He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him and upon Him we have relied. So you will know who is in clear error."﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who will bring you flowing water?"﴾.

[p. 302] Naafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Bazzi recited ﴿أأمِنتُمْ﴾ with the first hamzah realized and the second eased (tas-hil, softened); Abu 'Amr and Qalun inserted an alif between them; Qunbul replaced the first with a waw because of the preceding damma; and there are other options transmitted from him and from Warsh. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited both with full hamzah. "Him who is in the heaven" is a metaphor. The rational proof has established that He, exalted is He, is not confined to a direction. Its metaphorical sense is that His dominion (malakut) is in the heaven, because "in the heaven" is the complement (silah) of "man" (who), and in it is the pronoun that was in the governing element, which is "istaqarra" (settled). The meaning is: "He who is in the heaven is He," that is, His dominion. So there is an elision of a modifier (mudaf), and His dominion is in everything. But heaven is singled out for mention because it is the dwelling of His angels, where His Throne, His Footstool and the Preserved Tablet are, and from it His decrees, books, command and prohibition descend. Or this came in accordance with their belief, since they were anthropomorphists (mushabbiha), so the meaning is: "Are you secure from the one you claim to be in the heaven?" — while He is exalted above place. It has been said: "man" is by elision of a modifier, meaning "the creator of him who is in the heaven." It has been said: "man" refers to the angels. It has been said: Gabriel, who is the angel charged with the swallowing and other things. It has been said: "man" means "upon," and by height is meant domination and power, not place. In al-Tahrir: there is consensus that He is not in the heaven in the sense of settling, because whoever among the anthropomorphists and corporealists said He is upon the Throne does not say He is in the heaven.

﴿That He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾: that is, its going down into the depths, ﴿and behold, it shakes﴾: that is, it goes or undulates, as dust goes in the wind. The explanation of "hasib" (violent wind) has already been given in Surah al-Isra. "Nadhir" (warning) and "nakir" (rejection) are both verbal nouns, meaning "indhar" (warning) and "inkar" (rejection). Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"He warned Quraysh with sincere counsel of the like of it, from the Most Merciful, if it accepted a warner."

Warsh pronounced the final yaa in "nadhiri" and "nakiri," and the rest of the seven readers omitted it. When He warned them of what could be inflicted upon them of swallowing and the sending of the violent wind, He alerted them to take lesson from the birds and from how perfectly they were created, and to the incapacity of their gods in regard to any of that. This lesson from the birds fits, since mention of the violent wind had preceded it, and Allah destroyed the People of the Elephant by birds and by the violent wind they threw at them. So in this there is a reminder to Quraysh of this story, and that, exalted is He, had He willed, He would have destroyed them with a violent wind cast by birds, as He did with the People of the Elephant.

"Saffat" (spreading): extending their wings and keeping them in ranks until they seem still. "Yaqbidna" (folding): drawing their wings in to their sides. These are two states of the bird, resting from one to the other. He conjoined the verb to the noun when the noun is in the sense of the verb. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿So those who attack at dawn (al-mughirat subhan), and raise dust (fa-atharna)﴾; the verb was conjoined to the noun because the meaning was "those who attacked at dawn and raised dust." This kind of conjunction is eloquent, and the reverse is also permissible, except according to al-Suhayli, who considered it ugly, as in the saying:

"He keeps covering it with a cutting sword, one that aims in its flanks and deviates."

That is: aiming in its flanks and deviating. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Saffat" means spreading their wings in the air when flying, because when they spread them they align their primary feathers in a row. "Yaqbidna" means folding them when they strike their sides with them. He asked: "Why was it said 'yaqbidna' and not 'qabidat'?" He answered: The origin of flying is the arrangement of the wings, because flying in the air is like swimming in water, and the origin of swimming is extending and spreading the limbs. As for folding, it is an occurrence over the spreading, to gain support by it for movement; so what is incidental and not original was expressed by a verb, in the sense that they are "spreading," and folding occurs from them at times after times, as it occurs from a swimmer. End. Its summary is that the predominant state is spreading, so it is as if it were the fixed one, and was expressed by a noun; folding is renewed, so it was expressed by a verb. ﴿None holds them up except the Most Merciful﴾: that is, by His power. Al-Zamakhshari said: and by what He arranged for them of primary and secondary feathers, and by constructing their bodies in a form and with properties from which running through the air may come. ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of all things﴾, knowing how He creates and how He arranges wonders. End. In this there is an inclination toward the view of the naturalists (ahl al-tabi'a). We say: when He wills to hold up the heaviest things in the air and raise them to the Throne, that happens; and when He wills to bring down what is lighter, to the furthest point of descent, that happens; and that is not bound to any form, neither by heaviness nor lightness.

[p. 303] The majority read ﴿ما يُمْسِكُهُنَّ﴾ with light emphasis; al-Zuhri read it with doubled emphasis. The majority read ﴿أمَّنْ﴾ with the merging of the "m" of "am" into the "m" of "man," since the origin is "am man." Here "am" has the sense of "bal" (rather) only; because what follows it is an interrogative noun in the nominative position as subject, and this is a predicate. The meaning: "Who is your helper if He afflicts you with His punishment?" Likewise: "Who is your provider if He withholds His provision?" The meaning: no one helps you or provides for you. Talha read "aman" with the "m" lightened and its vowel transferred to the second, as the group did. The author of al-Lawami said: its meaning is: "Is this one who is an army for you to help you, or the one who provides for you?" So its wording is that of interrogation, and its meaning is reproach and rebuke. End. ﴿Rather, they persist﴾: they continue in ﴿utuw﴾ (insolence), in arrogance and obstinacy; ﴿and aversion﴾: fleeing from the truth because of its weight upon them. It has been said: "this" refers to their idols.

﴿Is one who walks prone on his face...﴾: Qatada said it was revealed describing the state of the Resurrection, when the disbelievers will walk on their faces, and the believers will walk upright. It has been said to the Prophet ﷺ: "How does the disbeliever walk on his face?" He said: "He who made him walk on his feet in this world is able to make him walk on his face in the Hereafter." So walking, according to Qatada's view, is literal. It has been said that it is a metaphor, struck as a parable for the disbeliever and the believer in this world. It has been said it is general, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak, that it was revealed concerning both of them. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and the Messenger, peace be upon him. It has been said: concerning Abu Jahl and Hamzah. The meaning: the disbeliever, in his agitation and perverse conduct in his belief, and the confusion of the matter for him, is like one who moves up and down, like a blind man who stumbles every hour and falls on his face. As for the believer, because his heart is at rest in faith, and the truth has become clear to him, he is like one walking with sound sight, upright, not deviating, on a road of evident straightness with no rough ground in it; his instrument of sight is sound and his path has no difficulty. ﴿Prone (mukiban)﴾ is a state (hal) from "akabba," which is intransitive, while "kabba" is transitive. He said: ﴿So their faces were thrown into the Fire﴾ [an-Naml: 90]. The hamzah in it indicates entering into a thing or becoming. The reflexive of "kabba" is "inkabba." You say: "I turned him over and he turned over." Al-Zamakhshari said: there is nothing of the form "af'ala" that is reflexive, and only the bearers of Sibawayh's book master this; and this man is much given to boasting about Sibawayh's book, and how many texts in Sibawayh's book have been blinded to his sight and insight, to the extent that the Imam Abu al-Hajjaj Yusuf ibn Ma'zuz wrote a book mentioning what al-Zamakhshari erred in and what he was ignorant of from the texts of Sibawayh's book. ﴿Ahda﴾ (more guided): an elative (af'al al-tafdil) apparently from "huda" (guidance), and it is like "Is honey sweeter or vinegar?" This interrogation is not meant literally; rather, what is meant is that every hearer would answer that the one walking upright on a straight path is more guided. ﴿Qalilan﴾ is in the accusative as an attribute of an elided verbal noun, and "ma" is superfluous; ﴿tashkurun﴾ is a new clause or a state (hal) presumed: "you give thanks, a little thanks." Ibn 'Atiyya said: its apparent meaning is that they give thanks a little, and what could thanks from the disbelievers be, which is little and not beneficial? But if he meant negation of thanks entirely, then he expressed it with paucity, as the Arabs say: "This is a land which rarely produces such-and-such," while it does not produce it at all. End. The like of his saying and the refutation of it were already mentioned in that place.

﴿Dhara'akum﴾: scattered you. "Hashr" is resurrection. The promise referred to is the promise of the Day of Resurrection, meaning: when is the fulfilment of this promise?

﴿Then when they see it approaching (zulfatan)﴾: that is, they see the punishment, which is what was promised to them. "Zulfah" means nearness, that is, one of nearness. Al-Hasan said: "in plain sight." Ibn Zayd said: "present." It has been said: the estimate is "a place of nearness," so it is in the accusative as an adverb of place. ﴿Sie'at﴾: that is, its sight distressed their faces, and evil and grief appeared in them, and blackness covered them, like one led to execution. The majority made the kasra of the "sin" pure, while Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Shayba, Ibn Wuththab, Talha, Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i gave it a "damma" tinge. ﴿It will be said﴾ to them, that is, the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniya) and whoever rebukes them say: "This is what you used to call for." The majority read ﴿tadda'un﴾ with the "dal" doubled and vowelled with fatha; it has been said it is from "claim" (da'wa). Al-Hasan said: "you claim that there is no Paradise and no Fire." It has been said: "you seek and demand hastily," and it is from "du'a" (calling). This view is strengthened by the reading of Abu Raja', al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Yasar 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim, Salam and Ya'qub: ﴿tad'un﴾ with the "dal" unvowelled; and this is the reading of Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Zayd, 'Isma (from Abu Bakr) and al-Asma'i from Nafi'. It is reported that the disbelievers used to call down destruction upon the Messenger ﷺ and his companions. It has been said: they used to plot among themselves to destroy them by killing and the like; so he was commanded to say: "If Allah destroys me" as you wish, "or has mercy upon us" by granting us victory over you, then who will protect you from the punishment that your disbelief has caused? When He said "or has mercy upon us," He said "He is the Most Merciful," then He mentioned what brings salvation, which is faith and entrusting oneself to Allah, exalted is He. The majority read ﴿fa-satalamun﴾ with the "ta" of address, while al-Kisa'i read it with the "ya" of the third person, looking at His saying: ﴿who will protect the disbelievers﴾. When He mentioned the punishment, which is the general mention of the loss of what gives life to souls, namely water, this is a specific punishment. "Ghawr" (sunken) is explained in al-Kahf, and "ma'in" (flowing) in Qad Aflaha. The answer to "if He destroys me" is "who will protect," and the answer to "if it becomes sunken" is "who will bring you," and this verse was recited in the presence of some of the mockers, and he said: "Bring it with the shovels and the hoes," and the water of his eyes departed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 67, verses 16–30:

The Exalted and Majestic One said: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you, and behold, it shakes?﴾ ﴿Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send against you a violent wind (hasib), and you will know how My warning was?﴾ ﴿And those before them had denied, so how was My rejection?﴾ ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seeing of all things.﴾ ﴿Who is this that is an army for you to help you, other than the Most Merciful? The disbelievers are not but in delusion.﴾ ﴿Or who is this that provides for you if He withholds His provision? Rather, they persist in arrogance and aversion.﴾ ﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ ﴿Say: "It is He who produced you and made for you hearing and sight and hearts; little are you grateful.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is He who multiplied you on the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you should be truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Knowledge is only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ ﴿But when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed, and it will be said, "This is what you used to call for."﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if Allah destroys me and those with me, or has mercy upon us, who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?"﴾ ﴿Say: "He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him and upon Him we have relied. So you will know who is in clear error."﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who will bring you flowing water?"﴾.

[p. 302] Naafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Bazzi recited ﴿أأمِنتُمْ﴾ with the first hamzah realized and the second eased (tas-hil, softened); Abu 'Amr and Qalun inserted an alif between them; Qunbul replaced the first with a waw because of the preceding damma; and there are other options transmitted from him and from Warsh. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir recited both with full hamzah. "Him who is in the heaven" is a metaphor. The rational proof has established that He, exalted is He, is not confined to a direction. Its metaphorical sense is that His dominion (malakut) is in the heaven, because "in the heaven" is the complement (silah) of "man" (who), and in it is the pronoun that was in the governing element, which is "istaqarra" (settled). The meaning is: "He who is in the heaven is He," that is, His dominion. So there is an elision of a modifier (mudaf), and His dominion is in everything. But heaven is singled out for mention because it is the dwelling of His angels, where His Throne, His Footstool and the Preserved Tablet are, and from it His decrees, books, command and prohibition descend. Or this came in accordance with their belief, since they were anthropomorphists (mushabbiha), so the meaning is: "Are you secure from the one you claim to be in the heaven?" — while He is exalted above place. It has been said: "man" is by elision of a modifier, meaning "the creator of him who is in the heaven." It has been said: "man" refers to the angels. It has been said: Gabriel, who is the angel charged with the swallowing and other things. It has been said: "man" means "upon," and by height is meant domination and power, not place. In al-Tahrir: there is consensus that He is not in the heaven in the sense of settling, because whoever among the anthropomorphists and corporealists said He is upon the Throne does not say He is in the heaven.

﴿That He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾: that is, its going down into the depths, ﴿and behold, it shakes﴾: that is, it goes or undulates, as dust goes in the wind. The explanation of "hasib" (violent wind) has already been given in Surah al-Isra. "Nadhir" (warning) and "nakir" (rejection) are both verbal nouns, meaning "indhar" (warning) and "inkar" (rejection). Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"He warned Quraysh with sincere counsel of the like of it, from the Most Merciful, if it accepted a warner."

Warsh pronounced the final yaa in "nadhiri" and "nakiri," and the rest of the seven readers omitted it. When He warned them of what could be inflicted upon them of swallowing and the sending of the violent wind, He alerted them to take lesson from the birds and from how perfectly they were created, and to the incapacity of their gods in regard to any of that. This lesson from the birds fits, since mention of the violent wind had preceded it, and Allah destroyed the People of the Elephant by birds and by the violent wind they threw at them. So in this there is a reminder to Quraysh of this story, and that, exalted is He, had He willed, He would have destroyed them with a violent wind cast by birds, as He did with the People of the Elephant.

"Saffat" (spreading): extending their wings and keeping them in ranks until they seem still. "Yaqbidna" (folding): drawing their wings in to their sides.
